topics.title: How the major parties are built, from the precinct up

points.text: Ohio law sets up each major party's county central committee with one member from each election precinct (or, if the outgoing committee chooses, one per city ward and one per township). Members are elected by direct vote at the primary in even-numbered years and serve two- or four-year terms, as party rules set.
The same Ohio section creates a state central committee of two members, one man and one woman, from each congressional or state senate district, as the outgoing committee decides.
In Ohio, a minor party's controlling committees are chosen under the party's own rules, not by the primary ballot that major parties use.

In Multnomah County, Oregon, precinct committee persons appear on the even-year primary ballot, only voters of that party and precinct see the race, and a candidate needs just three votes to win. Candidates must have been registered with the party for 180 days before the filing deadline, write-in candidates can file, and the term is two years.

Washington Democrats' precinct committee officers file with the county elections office during filing week, with no filing fee. A sole filer is automatically elected, and an empty seat can be filled by appointment from the county or legislative district chair. Precinct officers help elect local, county and state party leaders and nominate people to fill state House and Senate vacancies.

Why the seats matter: in Ohio, when a county office such as sheriff, auditor or commissioner falls vacant and its last holder was elected as a party nominee, that party's county central committee appoints the replacement, meeting 5 to 45 days after the vacancy.

topics.title: County and state party dinners and signature events

points.text: The Butler County (Ohio) Republican Party's 2026 Lincoln Day Dinner shows a typical ticket ladder: $150 single ticket, $1,500 table of 10, then sponsor tables at $2,000, $2,500, $5,000, $10,000 and $15,000. Higher tiers add VIP reception passes, program ads, signage, a thank-you from the emcee and a logo on the table. VIP-only admission is sold separately at $500.

Democrats' Jefferson-Jackson dinners are annual fundraisers; Tennessee's party chair called the dinner 'traditionally the largest fundraiser for a state Democratic Party.' By August 2015, Missouri, Connecticut and Georgia had dropped the name because Jefferson and Jackson were slave owners.

Rep. Jim Clyburn started his fish fry in 1992 in a parking deck near the South Carolina Statehouse. It thanked volunteers from his first congressional win and gave activists who couldn't afford the party's same-night fundraiser somewhere to go. It grew to draw about 1,500 people, and 22 presidential candidates were set to speak there in 2019.
NPR describes the fish fry as started to thank supporters who couldn't afford the state Democratic Party's high-dollar dinner. A cheap, open event beside the pricey dinner became the bigger draw.
The Harkin Steak Fry began in 1972 near Winterset, Iowa. With Iowa's leadoff caucus, it became a place for presidential campaigns to practise turning out supporters.

After Sen. Harkin's last steak fry in 2014, Democrats in Iowa's most populous county brought the event back at Water Works Park in Des Moines (reported October 2017), preparing 1,500 steaks, with members of Congress from three other states speaking. A county party can take over a signature event.

ActBlue has been around since 2004, founded by two friends who wanted to empower grassroots donors. By mid-2019 it reported nearly 7 million donors who had saved their details to give to any ActBlue campaign in one click.

ActBlue is a nonprofit run separately from the Democratic Party that processes gifts for Democratic candidates and liberal groups. WinRed, launched around the end of June 2019, was backed by President Trump's re-election campaign and Republican Party committees, and is built on the for-profit processor Revv.
ActBlue's Q1 2024 figures: about 2.4 million unique donors made 10.8 million contributions, averaging $42.73. Recurring gifts were 14.1% of volume (about $65.2 million), up from 12.7% in Q1 2020.

AP and OpenSecrets found that fewer than a third of Donald Trump's 2024 campaign contributions came from donors who gave under $200, down from nearly half in 2020. Per OpenSecrets data, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris raised $285 million from small-dollar donors from April 2023 on, more than 40% of their fundraising (reported October 10, 2024).

General-purpose platforms serve groups outside the two party pipelines. For example, Anedot's political product offers campaigns and committees recurring gifts, an option for donors to cover processing fees, event ticketing, a virtual terminal for entering offline gifts, and compliance-friendly data exports. It also serves nonprofits, churches and schools.

topics.title: Field programs, voter data and relational organizing

points.text: Gerber and Green's field experiment (American Political Science Review, 2000) randomly assigned about 30,000 registered voters in New Haven, Connecticut before the November 1998 election. Turnout rose substantially with face-to-face canvassing, slightly with direct mail, and not at all with phone calls.

Democrats' VoteBuilder (also called VAN) is the national voter database the DNC runs with each state party. In New York, campaigns and county committees request access and sign a user agreement, and the price depends on the number of registered voters in the district.

Republicans' GOP Data Center, originally built from the RNC's Voter Vault platform, gives users voter records from the RNC's national voter file plus tools to look up voters, build counts and lists, and export precinct call lists.

Relational organizing means reaching voters through people they already know. In Georgia's December 2022 runoff, a Democratic firm said it paid 1,455 Georgians about $200 each to contact over 58,000 potential voters, mostly friends and family. Firms involved claimed a 3.8% turnout boost in their network in the 2021 runoffs, which is a self-reported figure.

topics.title: Candidate recruitment and training, and how many seats there are

points.text: The Leadership Institute was founded in 1979 by Morton C. Blackwell to 'identify, train, recruit and place conservatives in politics, government, and media,' and reports training more than 161,000 people (figure as given on its Wikipedia page, undated).
Run for Something, launched in 2017, recruits and supports young progressive candidates for down-ballot offices. It reported a candidate pipeline of over 210,000 in June 2025.

Emerge recruits and trains Democratic women to run for office and has offered its program since 2002. Its signature training is 70 hours over six months, plus a weekend boot camp for active candidates.

EMILY's List (1985; 'Early Money Is Like Yeast') helps elect Democratic women who support abortion rights, raising money from members and giving candidates technical and strategic help in state and federal races.
GOPAC's Emerging Leaders program, begun in 2010, gives a selected class of elected Republican state legislators a year of training to prepare them for leadership in their chambers.

Example of a state party candidate school: the California Republican Party's 2022 'Parent Revolt' recruited and trained school board candidates. It offered virtual training, a binder covering filing deadlines, forms, vendors and how to spend campaign funds, and one-on-one sessions. It worked with county parties on attendee lists, and its April and July events each drew at least 100 people.

The 'about 500,000 elected officials' figure traces to the Census Bureau: its 1992 Census of Governments counted 511,039 popularly elected officeholders, including 18,828 in state governments, 491,669 across 84,955 local governments, and 542 federal.

Ballotpedia counted 76,902 elections in its 2024 coverage at all levels, excluding the presidency. 70% were uncontested, meaning no more candidates than seats. School boards were 49% uncontested, and November 2024 city council races were 65% uncontested, mayor races 71% and county commissioner races 64%.

A party usually gets on the ballot in one of three ways, depending on the state: a candidate passes a vote threshold, enough voters register with the party, or the party files a petition. It keeps that status by passing a later vote test or keeping a minimum registration. Ohio's vote test is 3%.

Petition requirements range widely: from 0.1% of registered voters in Hawaii to 10% of the last gubernatorial vote in California. Arkansas, Colorado, Maryland, Missouri and South Carolina each set a fixed 10,000 signatures, North Dakota 7,000, and many states use 1% to 3% of a recent gubernatorial vote.

Ballot Access News, Richard Winger's newsletter, noted in 2014 that in 38 states one petition puts a new party's nominees on the ballot for every office. Illinois instead needs separate petitions, about 25,000 signatures for a statewide slate alone.
As of September 2024, at least 186 Libertarians recognized by the Libertarian Party held elected office, per a list citing the party's own Elected Officials page.

Most Libertarian officeholders sit in nonpartisan seats. The party's 2013 count was 142 officials: 39 in partisan offices and 103 in nonpartisan ones. For nonpartisan offices, the party counts current or former dues-paying members or registered Libertarians, and state affiliates have latitude.

Nonpartisan local offices are the norm: the National League of Cities says over three-quarters of all municipalities hold nonpartisan elections, so city council and similar races carry no party label on the ballot.

topics.title: Campaign-finance basics a small party affiliate must know

points.text: Federal registration, state or national party committee: register with the FEC within 10 days of raising more than $1,000 in contributions, or spending more than $1,000 on contributions or other expenditures, in a calendar year. Registration is a Statement of Organization (Form 1).

Federal registration, local party organization: register if it raises more than $5,000 in contributions to influence a federal election, spends more than $1,000 on federal contributions or expenditures, or spends more than $5,000 on exempt party activities. Once registered, it is presumed affiliated with the state party and shares its contribution limits.
Party organizations must pay for all activity in connection with federal elections with money that meets federal contribution limits and prohibitions.

Federal rule 11 CFR 102.7: every political committee must have a treasurer, and it may not accept contributions or make expenditures while the treasurer's post is vacant, unless a designated assistant treasurer steps in.

State races follow state law, and states differ widely. As of February 2023, 11 states set no limits on individual donors, 19 put no limit on state party contributions to candidates, 8 apply individual limits to parties, and 19 set separate party limits.

A state-registered committee or unregistered local party that gives to federal candidates must use federally permissible funds, and may have to register with the FEC once its federal giving passes the thresholds.

topics.title: Bingo and raffles: usually charity-only, so partner with a charity

points.text: Ohio: a charitable organization applies to the Attorney General each year before January 1 for a bingo licence. It must show two years' continuous existence as a charitable organization in Ohio and an IRS determination letter under section 501(c)(3), (4), (7), (8), (10) or (19).

New York: a State Board of Elections enforcement determination, about a county Republican committee's 2021 raffle, states that political parties and other political committees are specifically not authorized organizations for games of chance, including raffles, under General Municipal Law section 186.

New Mexico: in 2019 the Gaming Control Board told the Los Alamos Republican Party to cancel a raffle planned for its fall dinner and refund tickets. The board said political organizations don't meet the definition of a qualified organization under the Bingo and Raffle Act.

Illinois is an exception: political committees may run raffles with a licence from the State Board of Elections. Only bona fide members may run the raffle, without pay, records must be kept for three years and reported, and all net proceeds go to the committee's lawful purposes.
